row.title: The Bay Colt Learns to Mind
row.author: Clara Dillingham Pierson

plot_extraction.response_text:
A stubborn Bay Colt resents advice, gnaws his manger, and repeatedly runs away from the pasture despite warnings. After the farmer fits him with a cumbersome device to prevent him from jumping fences, he recognizes his foolishness but later becomes defiant again when training begins.

While his obedient cousin, the Gray Colt, calmly accepts the bit and learns to pull, the Bay Colt fights the farmer, leaving his mouth sore and making his own life difficult. Seeing his cousin’s success leads him to reflect on his behavior. He stops cribbing, cooperates with his training, and soon works beside his mother at the plow. Proud of his straight furrows and his place among the working horses, he realizes that accepting guidance and useful responsibility is more satisfying than stubbornness and constant play.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts the style of a late nineteenth- or early twentieth-century didactic animal tale for children. It combines the conventions of a barnyard fable with realistic details of horse behaviour, anatomy, training, and farm work. Its central purpose is moral instruction: the Bay Colt’s resistance to advice causes avoidable discomfort, while patience, obedience, self-discipline, and willing work bring maturity and happiness. The lesson is stated openly rather than left implicit, especially in the narrator’s general observations about young animals learning to do right.

The narration is third-person omniscient, with free access to the animals’ thoughts, feelings, and motives. The narrator is warm, confident, and gently authoritative, frequently addressing the reader as “you” or appealing to shared knowledge through phrases such as “you know.” This creates the atmosphere of an adult storyteller speaking directly to children. The narrative voice regularly pauses the action to interpret behaviour, explain practical facts, or formulate a moral principle. It treats the horses as both animals and social analogues for people: they live in stalls, wear bits, pull ploughs, and display equine gestures, but they also reason, gossip, advise, sulk, feel pride, and negotiate family relationships in recognisably human ways.

The tone is affectionate, humorous, and mildly admonitory. The Bay Colt’s faults are presented as foolish rather than wicked, and the story never becomes harsh even when he suffers the consequences of his stubbornness. Humour arises from understatement, mock solemnity, and the translation of human social habits into horse terms. Examples include the Dappled Gray invoking the loss of the “black pits” in his teeth as proof of wisdom, the Colt’s pride in having unsplit hoofs, and the observation that two-year-olds often look more important than ten-year-olds and feel more so. The narrator’s irony remains gentle and protective, maintaining sympathy for the Colt while exposing his vanity and contrariness.

The diction is clear, domestic, and accessible, with occasional specialised equestrian vocabulary such as “halter,” “cribbing,” “curb-bit,” “snaffle,” “furrows,” and “plow.” Technical terms are embedded in explanatory contexts, so they enrich the farm setting without impeding a young reader. Capitalising animal names and categories—“Horse,” “Colt,” “Cows,” “Hogs,” and “Sheep”—gives the barn community the dignity of a miniature society. Characters are identified chiefly by colour, age, kinship, or physical trait rather than by personal names: the Bay Colt, the Gray Colt, the Dappled Gray, and the Blind Horse. This lends the story an archetypal, fable-like quality.

Sentence structure is generally fluent and moderately long, often linked by coordinating conjunctions and explanatory clauses. The prose has an oral storytelling rhythm, with repeated “and,” “but,” “for,” and “then” carrying events forward. Longer narrative sentences supply context and moral commentary, while dialogue is brisk, colloquial, and character-revealing. Repetition is used for emphasis and for a child-friendly cadence, as in “the next day, and the next day, and the next,” or the Gray Colt’s emphatic “I won’t go! I won’t go!” Contractions and idiomatic phrases—“Pooh!,” “Guess I know a thing or two,” “that’s all there is about it”—make the animals’ speech lively and informal.

Dialogue occupies a large part of the story and establishes character through contrasting verbal habits. The Bay Colt speaks boastfully, defensively, and in absolutes, repeatedly insisting that he can stop whenever he chooses or will never submit. The Gray Colt speaks modestly and sympathetically, acknowledging difficulty without using it as an excuse. The older horses employ proverbs, practical wisdom, restrained praise, and patient correction. Their speech reinforces a stable moral hierarchy in which age and experience deserve respect, although the elders ultimately teach most effectively by withdrawing unwanted advice and allowing experience to provide the lesson.

The plot is episodic but tightly unified around the Bay Colt’s maturation. An opening barn conversation introduces his cribbing and resentment of correction. A substantial flashback recounts his earlier fence-jumping and the humiliating wooden poke that cured him of running away. The narrative then returns to the present and develops the larger test of being broken to harness. Parallel treatment of the two cousins creates a clear contrast: the Gray Colt accepts guidance and progresses with relatively little pain, whereas the Bay Colt resists and develops a sore mouth. The climax is inward rather than dramatic, occurring when he recognises that his suffering is self-inflicted and resolves to change. The conclusion confirms his transformation through useful work, communal acceptance, and his mother’s forgiving maxim, “Colts will be Colts.”

Characterisation is broad, exemplary, and behaviour-based. The Bay Colt embodies youthful pride, contrariness, impulsiveness, and eventual capacity for self-correction. The Gray Colt serves as his foil, showing that goodness is not the absence of temptation but the decision to resist it; her admission that she “aches” to run away gives her virtue psychological credibility. The Dappled Gray is gruff but benevolent, the Blind Horse quietly wise, and the mothers concerned but patient. The farmer is depicted as firm, calm, and kind, never punishing in anger. This supports the story’s paternalistic worldview: legitimate authority is assumed to be benevolent, and submission to it becomes a route to competence and fulfilment.

Imagery is concrete and restrained, grounded in sensory details of barn and field: teeth grating on wood, a stem of hay dropping in sudden silence, ears moving restlessly, lines tightening against a bit, an apple core offered as a reward, and straight furrows opening behind a plough. Similes are simple and rural, such as a whispered breath moving through the stalls “like the wind passing over a wheatfield.” Animal gestures—snorting, whinnying, tossing the head, stamping, switching the tail, and arching the neck—function like human facial expressions and keep the anthropomorphism anchored in observed equine behaviour.

The dominant themes are obedience, maturity, self-mastery, responsibility, and the dignity of work. The story distinguishes coercive goodness from chosen goodness: the Bay Colt does not truly mature merely because he is restrained, but because he understands the consequences of his conduct and begins correcting himself. It also stresses that advice is motivated by affection, that freedom without discipline can become self-defeating, and that useful participation in a community produces pride and belonging. Overall, the style is earnest, orderly, reassuring, and explicitly moral, designed to entertain children through personified animals while guiding them toward socially approved habits of patience, humility, and willing cooperation.

## The Bay Colt Learns to Work

The Bay Colt stood in his stall with his forefeet planted wide apart, his ears laid back, and his strong white teeth fastened upon the edge of the manger.

Gr-r-r-r! went his teeth upon the wood.

“Don’t do that,” said the Dappled Gray from the next stall. “Cribbing is a bad habit, and a Horse who begins it may keep on until his teeth are worn and his manger ruined.”

The Bay Colt stopped long enough to turn one eye toward him.

“I can stop whenever I choose,” he said.

Then he began again.

Gr-r-r-r! Gr-r-r-r!

The Dappled Gray sighed. He was an old Horse, and the black pits had long since disappeared from his front teeth. He considered this excellent proof that he had learned a thing or two.

“That is what young Horses always say,” he remarked. “They think being able to stop and being willing to stop are the same thing.”

“Pooh!” said the Bay Colt. “You old Horses are forever giving advice. When I am as old as you, perhaps I shall give advice too.”

“It is likely,” answered the Dappled Gray. “And the young Horses will think you know nothing.”

The Blind Horse, who stood beyond the Dappled Gray, gave a soft whinny. “I used to think my dam knew very little,” he said. “Afterward I found that she knew nearly everything I had to learn.”

The Bay Colt pulled a splinter from the manger and dropped it on the floor.

“My mother worries too much,” he said. “She worries if I run, and she worries if I stand still. She worries if I eat quickly, and she worries if I leave a wisp of hay. It is a wonder her mane has not turned white.”

“Perhaps,” said the Dappled Gray, “you have helped her worry.”

At that moment the Bay Colt’s mother looked over her stall door. She was a handsome Bay Mare, broad across the chest and marked upon one shoulder by the smooth place where the harness had rubbed through many seasons.

“Son,” she said, “leave the manger alone.”

“I wasn’t hurting it.”

“You were hurting yourself.”

“My teeth are strong.”

“They may not always be.”

“There! Everybody is at it again!” cried the Bay Colt. He tossed his head so quickly that a stem of hay caught in his forelock. “I wish people would mind their own affairs.”

The Gray Colt, his cousin, was eating quietly across the aisle. She was nearly his own age, but she had a gentle way of listening before she spoke.

“They do it because they care for you,” she said.

“I did not ask them to care for me.”

The barn became very still. Even the Hens scratching in the loose straw near the doorway seemed to pause, although Hens seldom pause when there is any possibility of finding grain.

The Bay Mare lowered her head and said nothing.

Now the Bay Colt was not wicked. You must understand that. He loved his mother very much, and if anything had frightened her, he would have run to her at once. But young creatures often say sharp things merely because good advice has touched the sore place in their pride. Then, when the sharp thing has been said, they are ashamed to take it back.

So the Bay Colt nibbled at his hay and pretended not to notice that his mother had turned away.

The Dappled Gray changed the subject.

“I remember,” he said, “when this young fellow would not stay in the pasture.”

The Bay Colt’s ears came forward.

“That was different.”

“It generally is,” said the Dappled Gray.

The pasture lay south of the barn, where the grass grew sweet and thick beside a willow-bordered stream. It was a very good pasture, with water, shade, and enough room for the Colts to gallop until their tails streamed behind them. Yet the Bay Colt had decided that the field beyond the fence must be better.

The first time he jumped out, his mother called after him.

“Come back! There are young apple trees in that field, and the Farmer does not want them trampled.”

“I shall not trample them,” said the Colt. “I am only looking.”

He arched his neck and trotted between the rows, taking great care to set one hoof directly beside a tender root and another upon a little mound of freshly turned earth.

Soon the Farmer came and led him back by the halter.

The next morning the Bay Colt jumped out again.

“Son,” said his mother, “the Farmer has mended the fence. You know he does not wish you to cross it.”

“Then why does he put such interesting things on the other side?”

“What interesting things?”

“Things I have not seen.”

His mother might have answered that nearly everything in the world was something he had not seen, and that this was no reason for breaking fences. But she knew he would not listen, so she only switched her tail sadly.

That afternoon he jumped into the lane and trotted as far as the bridge. A wagon rattled around the bend, and the driver had to pull his team sharply aside.

“Whoa there, you foolish young rascal!” called the man.

The Bay Colt sprang into the ditch, splashed through the mud, and returned to the pasture looking as though the adventure had been planned exactly that way.

“Were you frightened?” asked the Gray Colt.

“Not at all.”

“Your knees are shaking.”

“I like to shake them.”

The next day, and the next day, and the next, he went over the fence. If the Farmer raised one rail, the Bay Colt jumped higher. If he strengthened a weak corner, the Bay Colt chose another. Every escape made him more proud of his cleverness, although it was the sort of cleverness that brings everyone trouble and does no one good.

At last the Farmer said, “We must keep that fellow safe in spite of himself.”

He brought out a stout wooden bar, fastened it by a strap to the Colt’s neck, and let it hang before his knees. Farmers call such a contrivance a poke. It does not hurt a Horse who walks properly, but it makes jumping a fence exceedingly inconvenient.

The Bay Colt looked down.

“What is this?”

“A reminder,” said the Dappled Gray.

“I don’t need a reminder.”

The first time he tried to leap, the wooden bar struck the fence. The Colt landed in a heap on the pasture side, very much surprised and not at all dignified.

The Cows lifted their heads and chewed thoughtfully. The Sheep crowded near one another. The Hogs, who consider nearly every mishap amusing if it happens to somebody else, grunted together by the trough.

The Gray Colt hurried to him.

“Are you hurt?”

“Certainly not,” said the Bay Colt, scrambling up. “I meant to do that.”

He tried again at another place. Again the poke caught, and again he came down where he had begun.

For several days he was forced to carry the clumsy thing. It bumped his knees when he hurried and reminded him of his folly whenever he lowered his head to graze. Before long he began to understand that it was not the Farmer who had made his life troublesome. The Farmer had only met one inconvenience with another. The real trouble had begun when the Bay Colt refused to remain where he belonged.

“If I had stayed in the pasture,” he thought, “I should not be wearing this miserable stick.”

This was a sensible thought, and sensible thoughts are the first signs of improvement. When the poke was removed, the Colt did not jump the fence again.

For a time he was modest about it. Then he began to tell the other animals that he had never truly cared to run away.

“I was merely testing the fence,” he said. “Now that I know it is sound, there is no reason to jump it.”

The Dappled Gray said nothing. Older Horses sometimes know that a lesson which has entered only through the knees has not yet reached the heart.

Summer passed, and the Colts grew. Their legs no longer seemed quite too long for them, their chests widened, and their soft baby coats gave place to sleek hair that shone in the sun. The Bay Colt was particularly proud of himself. He had four unsplit hoofs, a thick mane, and a white star in the middle of his forehead. He thought the star gave him a distinguished appearance.

Two-year-old Horses often look more important than ten-year-old Horses and feel more so.

One morning the Farmer came into the pasture carrying a halter and a light snaffle-bit.

The Gray Colt walked to meet him.

“What do you suppose he wants?” whispered the Bay Colt.

“To begin our training, perhaps,” she answered.

“I won’t have a bit in my mouth.”

“You have never had one.”

“That is how I know I won’t like it.”

The Farmer rubbed the Gray Colt’s forehead, slipped on the halter, and led her to the barnyard. Her mother watched closely but did not call out.

The Farmer let the Gray Colt smell the bit. It was a smooth metal bar with rings at either end, much milder than a curb-bit and suited to a young Horse. He touched it to her lips. She drew back at first, for metal tastes strange to a Colt who has known only grass, grain, wood, and the occasional stolen apple.

“Steady, girl,” said the Farmer.

The Gray Colt trembled. She did not understand what was expected, and the straps hanging beside her face seemed alarming. Still, she heard the quietness in his voice. When he placed a thumb gently in the corner of her mouth, where a Horse has no teeth, she opened her jaws, and the bit slipped in.

It felt cold and awkward. She rolled it under her tongue and tossed her head once.

“That’s right,” said the Farmer.

He did not ask much of her that day. He led her around the barnyard, taught her to stop when the line tightened, and praised her when she followed. Afterward he removed the bit and gave her an apple core.

The Bay Colt had watched from behind the fence.

“Well?” he asked when she returned.

“It was strange,” said the Gray Colt, “but not terrible.”

“You submitted.”

“I learned.”

“Those are the same thing.”

“No,” she said. “Sometimes one must submit before one can learn, but learning is what matters.”

The Bay Colt snorted. “I shall never allow anyone to put iron in my mouth.”

His turn came the following day.

When the Farmer approached, the Bay Colt swung away. The Farmer followed without haste. The Colt trotted to the far corner, then wheeled and trotted back, hoping to show that catching him was impossible.

It was not impossible. The pasture had corners, the Farmer had patience, and the Bay Colt had not yet learned that the creature who wastes the most temper is usually the first to become tired.

At last the halter was buckled around his head.

“I won’t go!” cried the Colt, setting his forefeet.

The Farmer pulled steadily.

“I won’t go! I won’t go!”

His feet slid through the dust. Then the Farmer slackened the rope, stepped to one side, and clucked softly. The Colt, surprised by the release, took a step forward. The Farmer praised him.

The Bay Colt had meant to resist every step, but resisting properly requires almost as much attention as obeying, and presently he found himself in the barnyard.

When the bit touched his lips, he flung up his head. The Farmer waited. When it touched them again, the Colt struck at the ground.

“Steady,” said his mother from her stall.

“I am steady!”

“You are standing on three legs and waving the fourth.”

The Farmer stroked his nose and tried again. The Bay Colt clamped his jaws. Then, because he was busy planning how tightly to keep them closed, he forgot the toothless space at the side of his mouth. The Farmer placed his thumb there, and in another moment the bit was between the Colt’s teeth.

The Bay Colt threw himself backward.

The reins tightened, and the bit pressed against the corners of his mouth. He sprang forward, and the pressure ceased.

Instead of noticing this, he jerked backward again. The pressure returned.

Thus the Farmer was trying to teach him a very simple thing: yield, and the discomfort ends. But the Colt insisted upon teaching himself a much harder one: fight, and the discomfort continues.

He shook his head, pulled, backed, and tried to rub the bridle against the gatepost. The Farmer remained firm and calm. He neither struck the Colt nor shouted at him, for anger teaches fear more readily than wisdom.

After a short lesson the bridle was removed.

The Bay Colt’s mouth was sore.

“I knew it would hurt,” he grumbled that evening.

“You made it hurt,” said the Dappled Gray.

“The Farmer pulled.”

“You pulled against him.”

“That is the same thing.”

“It is not,” said the Blind Horse. “A closed door and a Colt pushing against a closed door may be in the same place, but only one of them is wasting strength.”

On the next day the Gray Colt learned to turn. When the left line tightened, she bent her neck and stepped left. When the right line tightened, she stepped right. She made mistakes, of course. Once she turned all the way around and faced the Farmer, looking pleased.

“That was too much,” he said, laughing.

“I thought perhaps it was,” she told the Bay Colt afterward.

“Then you made a fool of yourself.”

“Yes,” she answered cheerfully. “But I know better now.”

There is a great advantage in being willing to make a small mistake while learning. Those who are too proud to do a thing imperfectly often never learn to do it at all.

Soon the Farmer put a surcingle around the Gray Colt’s body and ran long lines through the rings. Then came the breast collar, the traces, and the light drag that bumped softly behind her. She started when she heard it, but the Farmer spoke to her, and she went on.

The Bay Colt watched through the rails.

“I suppose you enjoy being ordered about,” he said later.

“No,” replied the Gray Colt. “Sometimes I ache to kick up my heels and run away. Yesterday, when the gate stood open, I wanted to gallop down the lane more than I can tell you.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“Because I knew the Farmer trusted me.”

The Bay Colt had no answer to that, so he bit the manger.

Gr-r-r-r!

His sore mouth hurt at once, and he let go.

His own lessons grew more difficult because he made them so. When asked to turn, he stiffened his neck. When asked to stop, he rushed forward. When asked to go, he backed. The Farmer fitted no cruel curb-bit to conquer him, but continued with the mild snaffle and steady hands.

After each lesson the Colt returned sweating and angry. The corners of his mouth became tender, not because the Farmer sawed upon them, but because the Colt dragged against the bit.

Meanwhile the Gray Colt was learning to pull a light cart. She stepped between the shafts, stood while the harness was fastened, and moved when the Farmer spoke. Her ears flicked backward to catch his voice, and she carried her head with quiet attention.

One afternoon she passed the pasture gate drawing the little cart. The wheels rolled smoothly, the harness shone, and the Farmer sat behind her with loose lines.

The Bay Colt called, “Are you tired?”

“A little.”

“Are you afraid?”

“Not now.”

“Would you rather be playing?”

“Perhaps for an hour,” she said. “But I am proud to know how to do this.”

The Bay Colt watched until the cart disappeared beyond the willows.

That evening he stood over his manger, but he did not gnaw it. The barn was quiet. Dusty bars of sunset slanted through the windows, and the Cows breathed slowly in their stanchions. Somewhere in the loft a Mouse rustled under the hay.

The Bay Colt thought of the poke. He thought of the bruises he had earned while trying to jump with it, and of the sore places in his mouth. He thought of the Gray Colt stepping freely under the harness, with no tight line and no angry tossing of the head.

“It happened before,” he said to himself. “I blamed the poke, but I had caused it by jumping. Now I blame the bit, but I am the one pulling against it.”

That thought was not pleasant. The most useful thoughts are sometimes unpleasant at first, just as a bit is cold when it first touches the tongue.

His mother looked over the partition.

“Your mouth troubles you,” she said.

“A little.”

She waited.

“I suppose,” he continued, “that I have been foolish.”

“A little,” said his mother.

He gave a short whinny which was almost a laugh.

“Why did you not make me behave?”

“You were made to stay in the pasture,” she replied, “but that did not make you wise. Wisdom begins when you choose what is right.”

The following morning, when the Farmer brought the bridle, the Bay Colt stood still.

He opened his mouth.

The Farmer’s eyebrows rose, but he said only, “Good fellow.”

At the first tightening of the left line, the Colt’s old pride told him to pull right. He felt his neck stiffen. Then he remembered his sore mouth and the Gray Colt’s quiet steps. He bent left.

At once the line softened.

“Why,” thought the Colt, “that is much easier.”

The next signal asked him to stop. He stopped. The pressure vanished, and the Farmer rubbed his neck.

There was no miracle about his improvement. He still forgot. He still became impatient, and once, when a Pheasant burst from the grass, he jumped so far sideways that he nearly stepped upon a trace. But instead of turning each mistake into a battle, he listened and tried again.

He also stopped cribbing.

“I thought you could stop whenever you chose,” said the Dappled Gray.

“I can,” answered the Bay Colt.

The old Horse moved his ears mischievously.

“And when did you choose?”

“After I found out that saying I could was not the same as doing it.”

The Dappled Gray nodded. “Your teeth still have their black pits, but there may be hope for you.”

By autumn the Bay Colt could pull a cart, back between shafts, and stand quietly at a gate. In the spring the Farmer harnessed him beside his mother to the plow.

The field smelled of damp earth. Larks sang overhead, and beyond the fence the Colts of that year raced through the pasture. The Bay Colt looked at them and felt the old desire to toss his head and gallop away.

Then the Farmer called, “Get up!”

His mother leaned into her collar. The Bay Colt leaned with her. The traces tightened, the plowshare entered the ground, and a dark furrow opened behind them.

At first he pulled too fast. Then he matched his mother’s steady stride. Down the field they went, and back again, while furrow followed furrow, straight and even.

“Well done,” said the Farmer at noon.

The Bay Colt looked across the plowed field. He had helped make those long brown lines. Soon seed would be dropped there, and rain and sunshine would turn it green. His shoulders were tired, but it was a good tiredness, very different from the weariness of fighting.

His mother touched noses with him.

“You are becoming a useful Horse,” she said.

“Were you ashamed of me before?”

“I was worried.”

“And now?”

“Now I am proud.”

He glanced toward the young Colts frisking beyond the fence.

“I behaved very badly.”

His mother switched away a Fly. “Colts will be Colts,” she said. “But they need not remain Colts forever.”

So the Bay Colt learned that guidance is not an enemy to freedom, and that work willingly done brings a pleasure which idleness never gives. He had not lost his spirit; he had learned to govern it. And that, you know, is one of the hardest lessons for young Horses—and for young people too.

### The Cartographer of Rain

In Bellweather, rain fell according to maps.

The maps hung in the Office of Civic Weather, twelve floors above the market square, where clerks in gray coats drew blue lines across parchment and sent the clouds obediently east or west. A circle over the orchards meant a morning drizzle. Crosshatching above the reservoir summoned three hours of steady rain. A black dot, used rarely, called for a thunderstorm.

Citizens spoke of weather as if it were a municipal service, like streetlamps or waste collection.

“Rain on the southern wheat fields by Thursday,” farmers would request.

“Clear skies for my daughter’s wedding,” a baker might plead.

“Fog along the river,” customs officers sometimes suggested, when they wished smugglers to grow careless.

At the center of this careful machinery sat the Chief Cartographer, an elderly man named Oren Vale. For forty-two years he had traced the routes of clouds. His hand never shook, his ink never blotted, and no storm had ever escaped the border of his design.

His apprentice, Mara Venn, admired him more than she admired anyone in the city, though she had never told him so.

Mara was twenty-three and thin as a compass needle. She had been born during a dry summer in the district of red roofs, the daughter of a laundress and a bellmaker. As a child, she drew maps of places that did not exist: forests beneath the sea, cities inside mountains, islands that migrated like birds. When she was fourteen, she discovered that some lines, drawn with the right intention, could persuade the world to change.

A spiral sketched on her bedroom window brought mist into the room. A narrow blue path painted on the garden wall made dew gather there each dawn. Once, without meaning to, she drew a storm over her schoolhouse and flooded the headmaster’s office.

The Office of Civic Weather hired her the following week.

By the time she became Oren’s apprentice, she knew every authorized symbol in the Weather Codex: the hooked mark for sleet, the three-pointed star for lightning, the pale wash that invited high clouds but no rain. Yet Oren taught her that the symbols were the least important part.

“A map is not an order,” he said on her first day. “It is a promise.”

“To whom?”

“To everyone beneath it.”

He gave her a blank sheet of weather parchment, made from linen, river reeds, and a secret powder that smelled like cold stone.

“Draw rain over the western gardens.”

Mara dipped her pen into blue ink and drew a neat oval around the gardens. Within it, she added the standard pattern for moderate rainfall.

Oren examined her work.

“How much rain?”

“Half an inch.”

“For how long?”

“Two hours.”

“Beginning when?”

“At noon.”

“And where will the clouds come from?”

Mara hesitated.

Oren pointed to the empty margin beyond the western wall. “Every rain has a history. You cannot place water in the sky without asking where it has been.”

She started again.

Over the years, Mara learned to chart not only destinations but journeys. She drew clouds from the sea, guiding them over salt marshes and chimney rows, lifting them above the cathedral spires before releasing them over gardens, fields, and tiled courtyards. She learned that clouds disliked sharp turns, that thunder was easily offended, and that fog had a fondness for abandoned places.

Most importantly, she learned restraint.

“The sky remembers every mark,” Oren often warned. “Draw only what you are willing to answer for.”

Then came the year when the sea stopped giving them clouds.

It began quietly. Spring arrived with pale mornings and weak winds. The reservoirs remained full from winter, and no one worried. Oren adjusted the maps, coaxing small clouds inland and rationing rain between the northern farms and the public parks.

By midsummer, the river had narrowed to a brown ribbon. Wells began to groan. Orchard leaves curled inward. Dust collected on windowsills and stayed there, undisturbed by drizzle.

Each morning, more citizens crowded the steps of the Office.

Farmers held baskets of shriveled fruit. Washerwomen brought empty buckets. Children stood with cups in their hands, though no one had told them to do so.

Inside, the clerks worked from dawn until midnight. Blue ink stained their fingers, cuffs, and faces. Every map failed.

They drew rain over the hills, but the summoned clouds arrived thin and exhausted. They charted storms from the southern gulf, but the winds tore them apart. They called fog from the river, only to watch it dissolve above the bridges.

Mara slept beneath her desk and dreamed of water.

Oren hardly slept at all.

One evening, after the other clerks had gone home, Mara found him standing before the great western window. Beyond the city, the sunset burned red through a motionless haze.

“Why won’t the rain come?” she asked.

Oren did not turn.

“Because there is none left to call.”

“That’s impossible.”

“No. Only inconvenient.”

He crossed the room and unlocked a cabinet Mara had never seen opened. From it, he removed a rolled map tied with black thread.

Unlike the city’s weather charts, it was drawn on animal skin. Its edges were burned, and the lines upon it seemed to shift when Mara looked away.

Oren spread it across the drafting table.

It showed Bellweather, the surrounding country, and the sea. But beyond the familiar coastline, far to the west, was a dark region shaped like a closed hand.

Mara leaned closer. “What is that?”

“The Hollow.”

“It isn’t in any atlas.”

“It was removed.”

“Places can’t be removed from atlases.”

Oren gave her a weary look. “You know better than that.”

Within the dark region, the map showed thousands of tiny blue circles layered one above another.

“Clouds,” Mara whispered.

“Every cloud that should have crossed the sea this year.”

“Why are they there?”

“Because someone is keeping them.”

Mara traced the coast with one finger, careful not to touch the ink. “Who?”

Oren retied the black thread around the map.

“My brother.”

His name was Silas Vale, and he had once been the most gifted cartographer Bellweather had ever known.

As they walked through the silent office, Oren told Mara the story.

When Oren and Silas were young, weather was less strictly governed. Maps were drawn by private guilds, wealthy landowners, military captains, and anyone else who could obtain the proper ink. Rain was diverted from poor districts to rich vineyards. Storms were aimed at rivals. A nobleman once kept sunlight over his estate for nine uninterrupted years, leaving neighboring villages beneath permanent cloud.

Oren wanted rules. Silas wanted freedom.

They argued in lecture halls, taverns, council chambers, and finally in the sky room of the old Weather Guild. Silas believed weather belonged to no government. Oren believed power without accountability would destroy the country.

In the end, the council agreed with Oren. The Office of Civic Weather was founded, private mapping was outlawed, and Silas was banished.

“He went west,” Oren said. “To a ruined observatory beyond the sea. I thought he had abandoned cartography.”

“But he’s hoarding the clouds.”

“So it appears.”

“Then we must stop him.”

Oren looked toward the dark windows. “Yes.”

They left Bellweather three days later aboard a narrow weather ship called the Petrel. Its sails were sewn with silver thread, and its deck was painted with symbols to soften wind and repel lightning. Captain Ilyen, who had transported Office cartographers for thirty years, agreed to take them west despite the empty sky.

The city rationed its remaining water while they were gone.

Each household received one jug a day. Public fountains were drained. Bathhouses closed. The bells of the cathedral rang only once at noon so the bell ropes would not wear out in the dry air.

At the harbor, Mara’s mother embraced her fiercely.

“Bring back rain,” she said.

Mara nodded, unable to promise aloud.

For five days, the Petrel sailed beneath a sky without a single cloud. The sea was flat and bright, a sheet of hammered metal. Flying fish broke the surface and fell back with sounds like small stones.

On the sixth morning, a black wall appeared on the horizon.

The Hollow.

As they approached, the air grew cold. Clouds towered behind an invisible boundary, packed together from sea to sky. White clouds, gray clouds, green-bellied storm clouds, purple thunderheads—all churned soundlessly within the dark region, unable to escape.

“Thousands of storms,” Captain Ilyen murmured.

“More,” said Oren. “Perhaps millions.”

Lightning moved through the Hollow like veins of gold.

The Petrel crossed the boundary at sunset.

Rain struck at once.

It did not fall gently. It crashed upon the deck in solid curtains, flooding the scuppers, flattening the sails. Wind seized the ship and spun it sideways. Captain Ilyen shouted orders while sailors climbed the rigging with knives between their teeth.

Mara clung to the mainmast.

“Oren!”

He was kneeling beside a deck table, trying to hold down a map. The parchment snapped and thrashed beneath his hands.

“Draw us a path!” he shouted.

“I can’t see the stars!”

“You don’t need stars. Listen to the rain.”

Mara shut her eyes.

At first she heard only chaos: water hammering wood, ropes cracking, thunder shaking the air. Then patterns emerged. Some rain fell heavier from the north. Some drops struck at an angle. Wind circled the ship, but not evenly. The storm was a maze, and every maze contained a route.

She crawled to the table.

With one hand gripping the rail, she dipped her pen. She drew the Petrel as a small silver shape, then marked the storm around it. Instead of commanding the wind, she described it. Instead of cutting through the clouds, she asked where they wished to go.

A narrow channel opened ahead.

“Now!” she yelled.

Captain Ilyen turned the wheel. The Petrel leaped forward, racing between walls of rain.

For hours, Mara continued drawing. When one map dissolved beneath the downpour, she began another. Oren held an oilcloth over her head, though the wind tore it twice from his hands.

Near midnight, they emerged into sudden stillness.

At the center of the Hollow stood an island of black rock. Upon it rose a single crooked tower.

Silas was waiting at the shore.

He looked enough like Oren to be his reflection in troubled water. He was taller, broad-shouldered, and dressed in a coat stitched with hundreds of weather symbols. His hair, unlike Oren’s white, remained almost entirely black.

“Brother,” he said.

“Silas.”

“You took your time.”

Behind Silas, stone steps climbed toward the tower. Along both sides stood iron poles bearing glass globes. Inside each globe, a tiny storm flickered.

Mara stared at them.

Silas smiled. “Beautiful, aren’t they?”

“You’re killing Bellweather,” she said.

“I’m teaching it thirst.”

Oren stepped between them. “Release the clouds.”

“No.”

“People are suffering.”

“People always suffer. The Office merely decides who suffers neatly.”

“We built the Office to prevent abuse.”

“You built a cage and called it fairness.”

Thunder rolled beyond the island.

Silas led them into the tower. Captain Ilyen remained with the ship, ready to flee if the storms closed around them again.

The tower’s highest room had no roof. Clouds rotated above it in a vast spiral. In the center stood a table carved from black stone, and upon the table lay a map larger than any Mara had ever seen.

It did not show the land.

It showed the sky itself.

Every cloud in the Hollow was marked there in moving ink. Lines of force bound them into circles, loops, and knots. At the center of the map, directly over the island, Silas had drawn a symbol resembling an eye.

“You made a prison,” Oren said.

“I made a sanctuary,” Silas replied. “Do you know what clouds dream of? Not wheat fields. Not wedding days. Not civic schedules. They dream of wandering.”

“So you trapped them?”

“I gathered them until the world remembers that weather is not a servant.”

Mara moved around the map. The craftsmanship was extraordinary. Every line had been drawn with precision, but something about it felt wrong. The clouds shifted and strained like animals caught in wire.

“They’re hurting,” she said.

Silas’s expression hardened. “They are clouds.”

“You said they dream.”

“That was poetry.”

“No. It was an excuse.”

For a moment, only the wind spoke.

Silas placed his hand near the eye symbol. “Leave now. I will open a route for your ship. In time, I may release enough rain to keep Bellweather alive.”

“How much is enough?” Oren asked.

“Enough to make the council beg.”

“And after that?”

“Enough to make them dissolve the Office.”

“And then every lord, general, and merchant will buy a cartographer.”

Silas shrugged. “Freedom is untidy.”

Oren glanced at Mara.

It was a small movement, but she understood.

While Oren stepped closer to his brother, Mara reached into her coat for a pen.

Silas saw her.

The wind struck before she could touch the map. It threw her against the tower wall. Her pen spun into the open air and vanished.

Oren lunged across the table. Silas caught his wrist. The brothers struggled over the moving map, careful even in anger not to tear it.

“Stop!” Mara cried.

Neither listened.

A drop of blood fell from Oren’s hand onto the parchment.

The map awoke.

Blue light raced through every line. Above the tower, the clouds began to descend. The spiral tightened, dragging storms toward its center. Glass globes shattered along the stairway. Miniature lightning bolts escaped and grew as they flew.

Silas released Oren and stared upward.

“What did you do?”

“Nothing,” Oren said.

But Mara saw the blood spreading through the ink. Weather parchment answered intention, and Oren’s intention had been tangled with rage, fear, duty, and grief. The map could no longer distinguish one command from another.

The cloud prison began to collapse.

“We have minutes,” Silas said.

“Then undo it,” Oren replied.

“I can’t. The master lines are merging.”

Mara ran to the table. The moving symbols blurred beneath the bloodstain. Every correction Silas attempted spawned another knot in the storm.

“There are too many commands,” Mara said.

“We must replace the map,” Oren told her.

“With what? We have no parchment large enough.”

Oren looked at the tower floor.

Black stone tiles spread from wall to wall, pale mineral veins running through them like rivers.

“A map does not need parchment,” he said.

Silas stared at him. Then, slowly, he understood.

Together, they overturned the table.

The sky map slid onto the floor. Mara seized a shard of broken glass and began scratching lines into the stone. Oren took another shard and worked beside her.

They drew the island first, then the sea, then Bellweather far to the east.

Silas remained motionless.

“Help us!” Oren shouted.

Silas looked up at the imprisoned clouds. His face changed—not softened, exactly, but opened, as if some locked room behind his eyes had finally admitted light.

He knelt and began to draw.

No ink joined the lines. Their blood did.

They cut their palms on the glass and traced routes across the stone: north to the mountains, south to the desert, east to Bellweather and the farms beyond it. They did not assign hours or quantities. They did not divide the rain by district or decree.

They drew only open roads.

The tower shook. Stones fell from the walls. Wind tore at their clothes and filled the room with salt spray.

At last, one route remained unfinished—the long eastern passage across the sea.

Mara reached for it, but Oren caught her arm.

“No,” he said. “Your hand is too weak.”

Only then did she notice how much blood she had lost.

“So is yours.”

Oren smiled. “I have been drawing this road for forty-two years.”

He pressed his palm to the floor and completed the line.

The effect was immediate.

The old map split down the center.

Above them, the clouds stopped.

For one vast, breathless moment, every storm in the Hollow hung motionless. Then the prison opened.

Clouds surged outward in all directions. They poured north, south, east, and west, roaring like rivers released from a broken dam. Some dragged lightning behind them. Others scattered into white fleets beneath the sun. Rain swept across the island, warm and clean.

The tower began to fall.

Silas lifted Oren from the floor. Mara led them down the shaking stairs as stones crashed around them. They reached the Petrel just as the upper half of the tower collapsed into the sea.

Captain Ilyen raised the sails.

Behind them, the Hollow vanished.

The voyage home took nine days.

Oren spent most of it in his cabin, feverish from his wound. Silas sat beside him, though the brothers spoke little. Sometimes Mara heard them arguing in low voices. Sometimes she heard them laughing.

On the seventh day, clouds overtook the ship from the west.

They did not attack. They traveled alongside the Petrel, changing shape in the afternoon light. One resembled a stag, another a ship, and another an old man with outstretched hands.

When Bellweather appeared on the horizon, bells began ringing across the city.

Rain had arrived three days earlier.

It had filled the reservoirs and soaked the wheat fields. It had washed dust from roofs, trees, statues, and faces. Children danced barefoot in the gutters. Adults stood beneath awnings, pretending not to weep.

The Petrel entered the harbor under a soft gray sky.

Mara’s mother was waiting on the quay. She pulled Mara into her arms, then held her away at arm’s length.

“You brought too much,” she said.

Mara laughed.

Oren retired from the Office before winter.

Silas was tried for weather theft, unlawful cartography, endangerment of the city, and several crimes so old the court clerks had to search the archives to spell them correctly. He admitted everything.

The judges sentenced him to twelve years of public service under supervision.

He became an instructor at the Office.

His lectures were extremely popular and frequently interrupted by Oren, who attended from a chair near the window and objected to nearly every point.

Mara became Chief Cartographer the following spring.

Her first act was to remove the black storm symbol from the Weather Codex. Her second was to open the Office roof to the public. Citizens could still request rain, fog, sunlight, or snow, but every request was written beside its cost. Rain for one field might mean less for another. Clear skies in one district might send clouds toward someone else.

Not everyone liked the change.

Freedom, Mara discovered, was untidy. So was fairness.

Years later, apprentices would ask how she had saved the city. They expected a secret symbol or a rare kind of ink. Some wanted to hear about the great sky map, the collapsing tower, or the storm roads scratched in blood.

Mara always gave them the same answer.

“A map is not an order,” she said. “It is a promise.”

“To whom?” they would ask.

She would lead them to the western window.

Outside, clouds crossed the city in their own time. Their shadows moved over mansions and workshops, gardens and prisons, temples and crowded streets. Sometimes they followed the routes Mara drew. Sometimes they did not.

“To everyone beneath it,” she said.

Then she opened the window and let the rain come in.
